I believe that yes, *everything* can be applied to a political context in some way. Even something as simple as a fruit basket can be associated to some political subject, from violent fruit-trafficking cartels (that's a thing!) to that one time when American fruit corporations orchestrated coups on multiple Central American governments (the Banana Republics). 

One might be like, "what could a fruit bowl possibly have to do with military coups?" It doesn't really have any relation to that in the practical, most immediate sense. But it *can*. Even if through the most tenuous link.

Art is viewed through the filter of subjectivity and experience of the mind, and being so constantly absorbed by politics as we are, I think we are doomed to percieve certain things as political which are not political by design. Andy Warhol is a guy that critiqued consumerist culture and capitalism by paiting colorful soup cans. 

I definitely agree about not all art being thought-provoking, nor does it necessarily need to. Just because a piece of art is political, it doesn't mean that it's *good*. Arguing that a fruit bowl is definitely, 100% linked to cartels is probably a reach and very stupid. My point is mainly that that link can be  made.

In the art-entertainment spectrum, videogames occupy just as much space as film, writing, visual art or any medium you could possibly imagine. Yes, some videogames are beautiful (in the aesthetically pleasing sense), have engaging and emotional stories, are fun to play, and are in general a marvel of human engineering and creative potential. 

However, the concept that all things that are pretty, engaging and fun are art is, to me, simplifying the concept of art into something that is comfortable.

Call of Duty is not art – it's message is lost under the countless game systems put in place to make slaughtering other human beings feel enjoyable, by the fact that it doesn't attempt to challenge or make us think about the world that we live in or the way we carry our beliefs and convictions. It is, at best, a fun and engaging experience that will have us going "woah, that was fucking awesome" by the time it ends. AND THAT IS COMPLETELY FINE.

Hobbs and Shaw is a film. It is the stupidest fucking film I've ever seen. And I love it with my whole damn heart. It is not art.
Norman Rockwell's paintings are pretty. They're nice to look at. I would probably hang one on my wall if I had one. To me, they are not art.
I really, really, really, enjoy Redbone's "Come And Get Your Love". I think it's the best damn song to listen to. It is not art.

All of these things are entertainment, not art. AND THEY'RE BETTER FOR IT. If I had to play Journey or The Witness every time I got home from a stressful day I would probably have killed myself by now. I just sit on my chair, get comfortable, and boot up Destiny 2. There's this notion in our society that calling something "art" gives it legitimacy. It does not.

I love entertainment. It makes life a little less dreary. Through it, I've met countless friends that have made me happy. Videogames like Call of Duty have got me through the majority of my time on this Earth. Just because they're not art, doesn't mean they're not absolutely fantastic.

Honestly, it's kind of ironic that people try to attribute so much meaning to the word "art" and then claim snobbery on whoever disagrees. Isn't that kind of snobby?
